title: What Liquid actually is (and isn't)
excerpt: Liquid is Shopify's templating language - server-rendered, sandboxed, and everywhere in your theme. The 10-minute mental model.

blocks.p: Liquid is the language Shopify themes are written in. Every product page, cart and collection you see on a Shopify store is Liquid being rendered on Shopify's servers into plain HTML before it reaches the browser.

Liquid takes data (products, collections, customers, settings) and outputs HTML. It runs on Shopify's servers, not in the browser - there is no JavaScript framework, no build step, no npm install. You write a .liquid file, Shopify renders it, done.

list: Objects - {{ product.title }} prints a value. Objects are the data Shopify hands you: product, collection, cart, customer, shop, and hundreds more.
Tags - {% if %}, {% for %}, {% render %} control logic. They produce no visible output themselves.
Filters - {{ product.price | money }} transforms output. money formats currency, default provides fallbacks, image_url resizes images.

blocks.p: Read it aloud: if the product is available, print its title in capitals and its formatted price. Otherwise show a sold-out message. That is 90% of what Liquid does - conditionals around data.

list: Not JavaScript - it never runs in the browser; {% javascript %} blocks are the exception, and they run as plain JS after render.
Not a database language - you cannot query or write data. You read what Shopify gives you.
Not theme-agnostic magic - every theme organises its files differently; Dawn's structure is not Impulse's.
Not unlimited - Shopify enforces render-time and memory limits; deeply nested loops can fail.

blocks.p: Next lesson: where all this code actually lives inside a theme, and how to navigate the editor without getting lost.

title: Inside a Shopify theme: files, folders and render order
excerpt: layout/, templates/, sections/, snippets/ - what each folder does, which files load when, and how a page actually gets built.

blocks.p: Open any Shopify theme's code editor and you see a folder tree. It looks arbitrary until you know the four folders that matter - everything else is configuration.

list: layout/ - the skeleton. theme.liquid wraps every page: <head>, header, {{ content_for_layout }}, footer. One file for the whole store.
templates/ - one file per page type: product.json, collection.json, cart.json, index.json. JSON templates (OS 2.0) list which sections render and in what order.
sections/ - the building blocks. Each .liquid file here is a section the merchant can add, reorder or remove in the theme editor - IF it has a {% schema %} block.
snippets/ - reusable fragments rendered via {% render 'name' %}. No schema, no editor presence - pure code reuse.

blocks.h: How a product page gets built

blocks.p: 1. Shopify picks templates/product.json. 2. That JSON lists sections in order - typically main-product, then maybe featured-collection, then footer. 3. Each section's .liquid file renders with the product object available. 4. theme.liquid wraps the whole result with header and footer.

Online Store 2.0 themes (Dawn and everything built on it) use JSON templates - sections are data-driven and merchants reorder them visually. Vintage themes use .liquid templates with hardcoded {% section %} and {% include %} tags. Most modern work targets OS 2.0, but knowing both matters because client stores run both.

list: Product-page feature? sections/your-feature.liquid with a schema block - merchant adds it via editor.
Reusable piece used in 5 places? snippets/your-piece.liquid, rendered with {% render 'your-piece' %}.
Store-wide change (announcement bar, custom CSS)? theme.liquid or a section group in the header/footer.
One-off page? Use a custom template or a section with page-targeted presets.

blocks.p: The GPLMart library follows this exactly: every snippet ships as one self-contained file - paste it in snippets/ or sections/, and the install notes tell you which. Lesson three covers the syntax you'll actually write.

title: Liquid syntax crash course: objects, filters, tags
excerpt: The complete working vocabulary - every object type, the filters you'll use daily, and the tag patterns that cover 95% of theme code.

blocks.p: This is the reference lesson - the syntax table you'll come back to. Skim it now, use it as a cheat sheet later.
Double curly braces print a value. Always safe - Liquid escapes HTML by default.

list: money - price in cents to formatted currency: {{ 199900 | money }} → $1,999.00
default - fallback when nil/false: {{ product.metafields.custom.subtitle | default: product.title }}
date - format timestamps: {{ article.published_at | date: '%d %b %Y' }}
image_url - resize CDN images: {{ product.featured_image | image_url: width: 600 }}
strip_html / escape - clean text for meta tags and JSON-LD
handleize / handle - turn titles into URL-safe handles
json - serialize for JSON-LD and data attributes
where / reject - filter arrays: {{ product.images | where: 'attached_to_variant?', true }}

blocks.p: {% assign x = value %} sets a variable. {% capture x %}...{% endcapture %} grabs rendered output into a variable - essential for building strings.

list: {% render 'name', key: value %} - modern, isolated scope, pass data explicitly. Use this.
{% include 'name' %} - legacy, shares parent scope, deprecated in OS 2.0.
{% section 'name' %} - renders a section inside a template/section (legacy themes).
{% stylesheet %} / {% javascript %} - embed CSS/JS inside a single file. This is how every GPLMart one-file snippet works.

blocks.p: You now have the full vocabulary. Module 2 applies it to the most valuable page type in ecommerce: the product page.

title: The product object & metafields: your data layer
excerpt: Every field on product.* explained, plus metafields - the structured data layer that makes custom features possible.

blocks.p: The product object is the richest object in Liquid - 60+ fields. You don't need all of them; you need to know which exist and which are metafields.

list: product.title, product.handle, product.vendor, product.product_type
product.featured_image, product.images (array of image objects)
product.variants (array: id, title, price, compare_at_price, sku, available, featured_image)
product.options_with_values (variant option names + choices)
product.price, product.compare_at_price, product.price_varies
product.available, product.selected_or_first_available_variant
product.description, product.content (richer HTML description), product.tags
product.metafields.namespace.key - custom merchant data

blocks.p: Metafields are custom data fields merchants (or apps) attach to products, collections, customers, shops - anywhere. A 'fabric composition' or 'fit guide' that isn't a native Shopify field lives in a metafield. In Liquid: {{ product.metafields.custom.fabric }}. In JSON templates, section settings can expose metafields via the editor's dynamic sources.

blocks.h: A practical pattern: spec table from metafields

blocks.p: This renders nothing when the metafield is empty - the {% if %} guard means the section silently disappears instead of showing an empty table. That pattern (render only if data exists) is how you ship features that work across a whole catalogue without touching every product.

product.price shows the *selected or first available* variant's price - but on a product with variants, the displayed price must update when the customer picks a different variant. That's JavaScript territory (product JSON + fetch). For Liquid-only work, use product.selected_or_first_available_variant.price for server-rendered accuracy, and know that real variant switching needs the AJAX API - covered in the cart module.
Next: turning this data into the components that actually move conversion - buy boxes, stock indicators and trust elements.

title: The buy box: price, stock, variants and the add-to-cart that converts
excerpt: Why the buy box area decides 80% of product-page outcomes - and the exact Liquid patterns for each element.

blocks.p: The 'buy box' is the cluster around the add-to-cart button: price, compare-at, variant picker, stock indicator, trust badges, delivery estimate. It's where purchase intent either survives or dies.
Note the minus filter computing the real saving - never hardcode '20% off'; the data already knows the truth.

Fake scarcity ('only 2 left!' on a store with 500 units) is both dishonest and legally risky in some jurisdictions. The honest version reads real inventory levels - but Shopify's product.variants[].inventory_quantity is only exposed when the merchant tracks inventory AND the theme has permission. Pattern: show urgency only when inventory is genuinely low.

'Order in next 4 hours - delivery by Thursday' outperforms generic shipping text because it answers the real question (when will it arrive?). Calculate cutoff from shop.metaobjects or a metafield; render only if configured.

Payment icons, returns policy, guarantee strip - placed directly under the buy button where hesitation happens. Every GPLMart product-page snippet (trust-badges, payment-badges, guarantee-strip, delivery-estimator) is built for exactly this slot - preview them in the playground before writing your own.

list: Create sections/buy-box.liquid on a dev theme
Render price + compare-at + save amount
Add the inventory-aware stock line
Add a {% schema %} with settings for trust-badge text and cutoff hour
Test with a product that has variants AND one that doesn't

blocks.p: Module 3 takes you into the cart - where the AJAX API unlocks everything dynamic.

title: Variants, options and product customisation fields
excerpt: Variant pickers, option swatches, file uploads and personalization - the inputs that turn a product page into a configured order.

blocks.p: Variants are Shopify's answer to 'same product, different choices' - size, colour, material. The Liquid challenge: render pickers that update price, image and availability without a page reload.

list: product.options = ['Size', 'Colour'] - option names
product.options_with_values = [{name:'Size', values:['S','M','L']}, ...]
product.variants[] = every purchasable combination with its own price, sku, image, available flag
variant.featured_media / variant.image - per-variant imagery

blocks.h: The classic pattern: variant JSON + JS

blocks.p: Server-render all variants as JSON in a script tag; JavaScript listens to picker changes, finds the matching variant, and updates price/image/ATC button. Shopify's own themes do exactly this. Liquid provides the data; JS does the switching.

code.code:
<script type="application/json" data-variants>
[
{%- for v in product.variants -%}
  {
    "id": {{ v.id }},
    "title": {{ v.title | json }},
    "price": {{ v.price }},
    "available": {{ v.available }},
    "image": {{ v.featured_image | image_url: width: 800 | json }}
  }{%- unless forloop.last -%},{%- endunless -%}
{%- endfor -%}
]
</script>

blocks.p: Colour options deserve swatches (visual), size deserves buttons or a dropdown. The variant-swatches snippet in the library renders colour swatches from option values with hex mapping via metafields or a settings JSON. For text options, styled radio inputs beat native selects on mobile.

Engraving text, gift messages, file uploads - things that change per order but aren't purchasable variants - use line item properties. Inputs named properties[Engraving] inside the product form flow through to the order automatically. No app needed for basic text personalization.

code.code:
<input type="text" name="properties[Engraving text]" maxlength="40" placeholder="Name to engrave">
<textarea name="properties[Gift message]" rows="2"></textarea>

blocks.p: These show up in the order admin and confirmation email automatically. The personalization-field and file-upload snippets in the library implement this pattern with validation.
You've covered the product page's data and inputs. Module 3: what happens after add-to-cart.

title: The cart object and AJAX API: making the cart dynamic
excerpt: cart.* fields, /cart/add.js and /cart.js - the endpoints that power drawers, upsells and mini-carts without reloads.

blocks.p: The cart object (cart.item_count, cart.total_price, cart.items[]) renders server-side on cart pages. But modern storefronts need a live cart drawer that updates without navigation - that's the AJAX API.

list: GET /cart.js - returns the whole cart as JSON
POST /cart/add.js - adds an item {id, quantity, properties}
POST /cart/change.js - updates quantities
POST /cart/update.js - batch changes
POST /cart/clear.js - empties the cart
Render the drawer markup hidden in a section (cart-drawer snippet does this)
On add-to-cart success: fetch /cart.js, re-render item rows client-side or re-fetch a rendered snippet
Show free-shipping progress: (cart.total_price / threshold) - pure JS math on the JSON
Open the drawer with a CSS class toggle - no library needed

blocks.p: Post-add upsells use the same /cart/add.js call with a 'continue shopping' vs 'checkout' choice. Pre-purchase upsells (before ATC) are simpler - they're just links that add a different variant. The cart-upsell and upsell-modal snippets implement both patterns.

list: Checkout itself (checkout page) is NOT customizable via Liquid on standard plans - Shopify checkout extensibility is a separate system.
Cart page IS a JSON template - you can rebuild it entirely.
Always handle the error response - /cart/add.js returns 422 with description when a variant is unavailable.
Debounce rapid clicks; double-adds are the #1 AJAX cart bug.

blocks.p: Module 4: making all of this controllable by merchants through the theme editor.

title: Building Flexible Sections with Dynamic Block Schemas
excerpt: Master section blocks in Liquid schema, from configuring repeatable item limits to adding interactive Theme Editor attributes.

blocks.p: Shopify section blocks empower merchants to add, reorder, remove, and configure repeatable content elements within a section. Rather than hardcoding fixed columns or rows, blocks allow flexible layout structures—such as sliders, feature grids, accordions, and custom icon lists.

Blocks are declared inside the JSON object within the section's {% schema %} tag. Each block entry requires a unique type identifier, a display name, an array of block-specific settings, and optionally a block-level limit or section-wide max_blocks restriction.

blocks.h: Rendering Block Iterations in Liquid Markup

blocks.p: In the HTML area of your section, iterate over section.blocks using a for loop. Access each block's settings via block.settings.setting_id. Crucially, you must append {{ block.shopify_attributes }} to the container element of each block inside the loop so the Theme Editor JS engine can highlight blocks live during customization.

code.code:
{% if section.settings.heading != blank %}

{{ section.settings.heading | escape }}

{% endif %}
{% for block in section.blocks %}
{% case block.type %} {% when 'feature_card' %} {% if block.settings.image != blank %} {{ block.settings.image | image_url: width: 600 | image_tag: loading: 'lazy', class: 'feature-grid__image' }} {% endif %}

{{ block.settings.title }}

{{ block.settings.description }}
{% endcase %}
{% endfor %}

list: Always include {{ block.shopify_attributes }} on the root wrapper of each block in your loop to enable active selection in the Theme Editor preview.
Use block types efficiently with dynamic Liquid case statements when supporting multiple block styles (e.g., image card vs. text column).
Define default blocks inside section presets so the section looks populated immediately when added by a merchant.
Set reasonable max_blocks limits to protect grid layouts from breaking on narrow viewports.
